Extra East: HART Railroad answer key

Every question in Extra East: HART Railroad, by shift and run: 188 in all, with a rule that comes up on several runs listed under each. Each shows its choices in alphabetical order with the right one ticked, and the rule behind it. Some questions come up only on some draws. The rules are in the C&E study deck.

188 questions

[varies] stands for a word that changes from draw to draw, such as a time or a count.

On the island: #105 ore job · #110 furnace job · #115 relief job · #205 second trick · #305 midnight job · EXTRA called off the extra board · YM yardmaster at South Yard
Up the Chartiers: Extra 4619 South the coal extra · No 307 South the passenger train · PC&Y Transfer the ore transfer · PIR Local the south turn

On the island Pittsburgh & Ohio Valley · 1979 to 1990

#105, ore job a weekday in 1981 · 12 questions

1 · GCOR 1.47A · GCOR crew & speed

Whose instructions?

The engineer has his own way of making up a drag, and the regular conductor has told him to make it up another way. The trainmaster asks you: for the work on the switching order, whose instructions does the crew follow?

  • The brakeman's, who is on the ground
  • The conductor's, unless they endanger the safety of the train or violate the rules
  • The engineer's, on everything
  • The senior man's, whatever his job

GCOR 1.47A: the conductor supervises the operation and administration of the train; everyone on it obeys the conductor's instructions unless they endanger the train's safety or violate the rules. On operating the engine itself, the crew obey the engineer (1.47B).

GCOR 1.47A

2 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

The track gang at S1

The track gang is working at the west end of S1, beside the South Runner. #4 is ready to move, and the trainmaster asks what the engineer does first.

  • Move at restricted speed without a signal
  • Nothing: these are not main tracks
  • Ring the bell only
  • Sound the required whistle signal before moving

GCOR 5.8.2: the whistle may be used at any time as a warning regardless of any whistle prohibitions. When other employees are working in the immediate area, sound the required whistle signal before moving.

GCOR 5.8.2

3 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

Engine or train?

The drag is ready: ten loaded hoppers, #4 on the west end shoving east, the brakeman riding the fifth car (blog, p.84). There is no marker on the rear, and you will stay on plant track. The conductor asks you to fill in the card: under GCOR, what is the movement?

  • A train, because it has cars
  • A work train
  • An engine with cars, not a train
  • An extra train

GCOR glossary: a train is one or more engines coupled, with or without cars, displaying a marker, and authorized to operate on a main track. An engine is a unit propelled by any form of energy.

GCOR Glossary

4 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

Backing up

#4 stands with its cab to the east, coupled to the drag. To shove east toward the dumper, the engine backs up. The conductor asks which whistle signal the engineer sounds before the move.

  • One long sound (—): air brakes applied
  • Three short sounds (o o o): when stopped, back up
  • Two long sounds (— —): release brakes, proceed
  • Two short sounds (o o): acknowledgment

GCOR 5.8.2: (5) o o o, when stopped, back up. (3) — — is release brakes and proceed, (4) o o an acknowledgment, (2) — air brakes applied, pressure equalized.

GCOR 5.8.2

5 · GCOR 6.28 · GCOR crew & speed

Up to the coke yard switch

You shove the drag along the plant tracks toward the coke yard switch. This is not main track and there are no block signals. The trainmaster asks at what speed.

  • A speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision
  • Not over 10 MPH, whatever the view ahead
  • Restricted speed, not over 20 MPH, looking out for broken rail
  • Yard speed, unless the track is known to be clear

GCOR 6.28: except on a main track or where a block system is in effect, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment fouling the track, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly.

GCOR 6.28

6 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

The switch with the yellow bowl

The coke yard switch has its bowl painted yellow. The brakeman calls that the drag trailed through it on the last trip and nobody lined it back. The conductor asks you where its points are.

  • Back in their first position, returned by a spring
  • Half open, until the next movement
  • Locked in the reversed position
  • Where the wheels forced them, so it must be lined back by hand

GCOR glossary: a variable switch, marked with a V or a bowl painted yellow, leaves the points where they were forced when it is trailed through. A spring switch returns them to their original position.

GCOR Glossary

7 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

The ore yard

At the dumper the hoppers are turned over on E2, and a car rider takes the empties down the hill in strings, braking by hand (blog, p.39). The tracks they come down to are used for storing cars and making up drags. The trainmaster asks what GCOR calls them.

  • A siding
  • A yard: tracks other than main tracks and sidings, used for making up trains, storing cars and other purposes
  • Main track, since the drags run on it
  • Yard limits

GCOR glossary: a yard is a system of tracks, other than main tracks and sidings, used for making up trains, storing cars and other purposes. Yard limits are a portion of main track designated by signs and special instructions or a track bulletin.

GCOR Glossary

8 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

At the fuel track

Between drags #4 goes to South Yard for fuel (blog, p.58). You leave the cut on the lead, and the last hopper stops between the clearance point and the switch points. The conductor asks you what that is.

  • A cut in the clear
  • A reverse movement
  • Equipment fouling a track
  • Working limits

GCOR glossary: equipment fouling a track is the end of rolling equipment left between the clearance point and the switch points leading to the track on which the equipment is standing.

GCOR Glossary

9 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

Men by the coke plant lead

Shoving drag 2, you come up on the track gang working beside the coke plant lead. The conductor asks what the engineer sounds.

  • A succession of short sounds
  • Long, short (— o), then two shorts (o o) at intervals until the head end has passed them
  • Nothing: plant track has no whistle rules
  • Two long sounds

GCOR 5.8.2, signal (8): approaching men or equipment on or near the track, regardless of whistle prohibitions, sound — o, then (4) intermittently until the head end has passed them.

GCOR 5.8.2

10 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

The last empties

The last string of empties comes down and the conductor has you set it on the West Yard track off the ladder. Where must the last car stand?

  • Anywhere, as long as the switch is lined back
  • Clear of the clearance point: where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass on the adjacent track
  • Just past the switch points
  • One car length from the switch, whatever the track

GCOR glossary: the clearance point is the location closest to a switch where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass equipment on an adjacent track.

GCOR Glossary

11 · GCOR 5.8.1 · Signals & whistles

The main crossing

Drag 3 goes over the main crossing, the road crossing by the yard office. The trainmaster asks when the engineer rings the bell.

  • From the yard office to the dumper, the whole way
  • Only if road traffic is in sight
  • Only on a train, not an engine with cars
  • Start at the crossing sign and ring until the crossing is occupied

GCOR 5.8.1: ring the bell before moving (except momentary stop-and-start switching), as a warning when necessary, approaching men or equipment, and approaching public crossings, starting at the sign and ringing until the crossing is occupied.

GCOR 5.8.1

12 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

The car knocker

The car knocker is inspecting hoppers on the next track. #4 is ready to move, and the trainmaster asks what the engineer does first.

  • Move at restricted speed without a signal
  • Nothing: these are not main tracks
  • Ring the bell only
  • Sound the required whistle signal before moving

GCOR 5.8.2: the whistle may be used at any time as a warning regardless of any whistle prohibitions. When other employees are working in the immediate area, sound the required whistle signal before moving.

GCOR 5.8.2

#110, furnace job January 1984 · 13 questions

13 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

Rail and road

You pull furnace coke from the battery. It goes over the yard office scale before F1 (blog, p.130), and on the way it crosses the road at the main crossing, rail and road on the same level. What does GCOR call that?

  • A crossing at grade
  • A crossover
  • A whistle quiet zone
  • Interlocking limits

GCOR glossary: crossings at grade are crossings that intersect at the same level. A crossover is a track connection between two adjacent tracks.

GCOR Glossary

14 · GCOR 5.8.1 · Signals & whistles

The main crossing

The coke string comes up to the main crossing, the road crossing by the yard office. When does the engineer ring the bell?

  • Not at all on plant track
  • Only if road traffic is in sight
  • Only on a train, not an engine with cars
  • Start at the crossing sign and ring until the crossing is occupied

GCOR 5.8.1: ring the bell approaching public crossings, starting at the sign and ringing until the crossing is occupied.

GCOR 5.8.1

15 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

Off the scale

The coke string is on the Toledo scale. You cut away and back off so the weight can be read; the trainmaster has the buzzer going before you are clear (blog, p.95). #4 is stopped facing the scale. Which whistle signal before backing away?

  • Four short sounds (o o o o)
  • Three short sounds (o o o): when stopped, back up
  • Two long sounds (— —)
  • Two short sounds (o o)

GCOR 5.8.2: (5) o o o, when stopped, back up. (3) — — is release brakes, proceed; (4) o o an acknowledgment; (6) o o o o a request for a signal to be given or repeated.

GCOR 5.8.2

16 · GCOR 1.47A · GCOR crew & speed

Riding the lead hopper

You ride the lead hopper of the coke string up to F1, as the furnace job's conductors did (blog, p.130). The weigh slip is in your pocket. Who answers for the coke reaching the furnace with its paperwork?

  • The conductor: freight conductors are responsible for the freight and its documents to destination
  • The engineer
  • The furnace foreman, once it is on F1
  • The yard clerk who weighed it

GCOR 1.47A: freight conductors are responsible for the freight carried by their train and for ensuring it is delivered with any accompanying documents to its destination, and they maintain any required records.

GCOR 1.47A

17 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

From E6 to E4

The ladles are rarely in the order the furnace wants, so you switch them from E6 to E4 (blog, p.91). The move from one track to the other goes through two switches joined by a short track. What is that connection?

  • A crossover
  • A dual control switch
  • A siding
  • A spring switch

GCOR glossary: a crossover is a track connection between two adjacent tracks, consisting of two switches, intended to be used primarily for crossing over from one track to the other.

GCOR Glossary

18 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

Working limits on E9

You need one more hot ladle off E9. The track gang's foreman has working limits on the track. How may #6 move inside them?

  • At restricted speed, not over 20 MPH
  • Freely, since it is not main track
  • Only after sounding signal (8)
  • Only as permitted by the employee in charge of the working limits

GCOR glossary: working limits are a segment of track within definite boundaries on which movements may be made only as permitted by the employee in charge.

GCOR Glossary

19 · GCOR 1.47B · GCOR crew & speed

Hot metal

You take hot metal out of the ladle house two ladles at a time; with more weight the cut can run on to the quench car at the battery (blog, p.14). Before the move, what must the engineer check with you?

  • Nothing: the ladle house sets the weight
  • Only the ladle numbers for the time sheet
  • The weights from the scale
  • Whether any cars need special handling

GCOR 1.47B: the engineer must check with the conductor whether any cars or units need special handling.

GCOR 1.47B

20 · GCOR 6.28 · GCOR crew & speed

B is still casting

It is past [varies] and B is still casting. You back toward the rear of the Furnace Runner to wait short of the bumping block, as the crews did (blog, p.14), in graphite dust that hides the block until you are close. At what speed?

  • A speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision
  • Not over 10 MPH, whatever the view ahead
  • Restricted speed, not over 20 MPH, looking out for broken rail
  • Yard speed, unless the track is known to be clear

GCOR 6.28: except on a main track or where a block system is in effect, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment fouling the track, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly.

GCOR 6.28

21 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

Air applied

Three ladles are out of the house: one for the foundry, one for the pig machine, one for recast (blog, p.138). You stop with them and the engineer makes an air brake application. Which whistle signal means stopped, air brakes applied, pressure equalized?

  • A succession of short sounds
  • One long sound (—)
  • Two long sounds (— —)
  • Two short sounds (o o)

GCOR 5.8.2: (2) —, when stopped, air brakes applied, pressure equalized. (3) — — is release brakes, proceed.

GCOR 5.8.2

22 · GCOR 5.8.2(7) · Signals & whistles

The Gulf Crossing

Iron for the foundry, at the other end of the island, leaves by the pig-yard lead at the Gulf Crossing. Your move starts a few car lengths from the crossing. No road traffic is approaching or stopped there. Must the crossing signal start 15 seconds before you enter?

  • No signal is needed at a plant crossing
  • No: starting less than 1/4 mile away, it may be sounded less than 15 seconds before when no traffic is approaching or stopped
  • Yes, and from 1/4 mile away
  • Yes: always 15 to 20 seconds

GCOR 5.8.2(7): when a movement starts less than 1/4 mile from a crossing, the signal may be sounded less than 15 seconds before the crossing when it is clearly seen traffic is not approaching or stopped at the crossing, or when crossing gates are fully lowered.

GCOR 5.8.2(7)

23 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

At the Y Interchange

Empty ladles and gons change roads with the PC&Y here, and you bleed the air off them first (blog, p.105). Done, the brakeman signals you ahead. Which whistle signal means release brakes, proceed?

  • Long, short (— o)
  • One long sound (—)
  • Three short sounds (o o o)
  • Two long sounds (— —)

GCOR 5.8.2: (3) — —, release brakes, proceed. (2) — is stopped, air brakes applied, pressure equalized.

GCOR 5.8.2

24 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

The East Runner Main

At A furnace the pig machine drops bars into gondolas two loads at a time. You pull the two loads and keep the safety car clear of the East Runner (blog, p.110). The East Runner Main is a track through the plant that must not be occupied without authority or protection. What is it?

  • A siding
  • A yard track
  • Main track
  • Working limits

GCOR glossary: main track is a track extending through yards and between stations that must not be occupied without authority or protection.

GCOR Glossary

25 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

On E1's grade

E1 is a steep grade with a lot of weight on it. You leave the pig iron loads there for the barge, but the last car stands between the clearance point and the switch points of E1. What is that?

  • A cut in the clear
  • A reverse movement
  • Equipment fouling a track
  • Working limits

GCOR glossary: equipment fouling a track is the end of rolling equipment left between the clearance point and the switch points leading to the track on which the equipment is standing.

GCOR Glossary

#115, relief job a Saturday in August 1979 · 9 questions

26 · Yard Limits guide · Yard limits

Who is in charge?

With no trainmaster or yardmaster on duty, who is generally in charge inside the yard limits?

  • Nobody; every crew works alone
  • The PC&Y crew, as the connecting road
  • The conductor or switch crew foreman of the first train there
  • Whoever has the most seniority on the island

Yard Limits guide: inside yard limits the yardmaster or agent is in charge if one is on duty; otherwise generally the conductor or switch crew foreman of the first train there.

Yard Limits guide

27 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

Who is crew?

The car knocker, the yard clerk and your brakeman are all at South Yard this morning. Which of them is a crew member under GCOR?

  • All three
  • The brakeman
  • The car knocker
  • The yard clerk

GCOR glossary: crew members are conductors, assistant conductors, brakemen, engineers, remote control operators, yard engine foremen, switchmen, and yard helpers.

GCOR Glossary

28 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

Lost in the dust

Shoving toward the dumper, the engineer loses sight of the brakeman's hand signal in the dust and cannot tell what it was. Which whistle signal asks for it again?

  • A succession of short sounds
  • Four short sounds (o o o o): request for a signal to be given or repeated
  • Three short sounds (o o o)
  • Two short sounds (o o)

GCOR 5.8.2: (6) o o o o, request for a signal to be given or repeated. (4) o o is an acknowledgment and (5) o o o is back up.

GCOR 5.8.2

29 · GCOR 1.47B · GCOR crew & speed

Tank cars

[varies] loaded tank cars from USS Chemicals are going out to the PC&Y. What must the engineer check with the conductor before handling them?

  • Nothing: that is the conductor's paperwork
  • Only the car numbers for the time sheet
  • The weights, before they are weighed
  • Whether any cars need special handling

GCOR 1.47B: the engineer must check with the conductor whether any cars or units need special handling.

GCOR 1.47B

30 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

S9

You run around the tank cars on S9, just west of the scale, where outbound tank cars were run around (blog, p.90). Is S9 a siding?

  • No: a siding is connected to the main track, used for meeting or passing trains, and shown in the timetable
  • Only when a train uses it
  • Yes, because it parallels the scale track
  • Yes: any track used to run around cars is a siding

GCOR glossary: a siding is a track connected to the main track and used for meeting or passing trains; sidings are shown in the timetable.

GCOR Glossary

31 · GCOR 6.28 · GCOR crew & speed

The scale is thrown red

You start to roll the tank cars toward the scale. The signal at the scale has been thrown red. What do you do?

  • Back off and go around by the East Runner
  • Keep rolling at a walk: it only means weighing is in progress
  • Sound two shorts and go across
  • Stop short of it: the move must be able to stop short of a stop signal

GCOR 6.28: off main track, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment fouling the track, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly. Mark Connolly thought the scale had been thrown red in the 1979 photo of #6.

GCOR 6.28

  • Clear of the clearance point: where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass on the adjacent track
  • Just past the switch points
  • One car length from the switch, whatever the track

GCOR glossary: the clearance point is the location closest to a switch where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass equipment on an adjacent track.

You take the weighed coke up the furnace lead to F1. No block signals, not main track. At what speed?

  • A speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision
  • Not over 10 MPH, whatever the view ahead
  • Restricted speed, not over 20 MPH, looking out for broken rail
  • Yard speed, unless the track is known to be clear

GCOR 6.28: except on a main track or where a block system is in effect, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment fouling the track, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly.

Over the scale

The tank cars go over the Toledo scale at a walk; the weight is read the moment you cut away and back off (blog, p.95). The scale track is plant track. At what speed?

  • A speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision
  • Not over 10 MPH, whatever the view ahead
  • Restricted speed, not over 20 MPH, looking out for broken rail

GCOR 6.28: except on a main track or where a block system is in effect, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment fouling the track, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly.

#205, second trick an evening in 1987 · 8 questions

35 · GCOR 1.46 · GCOR crew & speed

The trainmaster's orders

A yardmaster is on duty tonight. Under GCOR, whose instructions do the yard crews follow?

  • The PC&Y conductor's at the interchange
  • The conductor's, on everything
  • The engineer's, who runs the engine
  • The yardmaster's: he directly supervises the yard crews

GCOR 1.46: the yardmaster directly supervises yard crews, clerks and others in the yard, and where a yardmaster is on duty, train, engine and yard crews follow the yardmaster's instructions. On the P&OV the trainmaster wrote the switching orders.

GCOR 1.46

36 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

A lantern in the dusk

The brakeman gives a lantern signal that the engineer understands and there is no whistle signal for it. How does the engineer acknowledge it?

  • Four short sounds (o o o o)
  • One long sound (—)
  • Two long sounds (— —)
  • Two short sounds (o o)

GCOR 5.8.2: (4) o o, acknowledgment of any signal not otherwise provided for.

GCOR 5.8.2

37 · GCOR Glossary · Definitions

At Stucki

An occasional boxcar for Stucki. You spot it at the plant. Where must it stand so the next move can pass it?

  • Anywhere, as long as the switch is lined back
  • Clear of the clearance point: where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass on the adjacent track
  • Just past the switch points
  • One car length from the switch, whatever the track

GCOR glossary: the clearance point is the location closest to a switch where it is safe for equipment, and a person riding the side of equipment, to pass equipment on an adjacent track.

GCOR Glossary

38 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

The car knocker at Aristech

The car knocker is still working between two of the Aristech tank cars when your engine is ready to couple. What does the engineer do first?

  • Move at restricted speed without a signal
  • Nothing: these are not main tracks
  • Ring the bell only
  • Sound the required whistle signal before moving

GCOR 5.8.2: the whistle may be used at any time as a warning regardless of any whistle prohibitions. When other employees are working in the immediate area, sound the required whistle signal before moving.

GCOR 5.8.2

39 · GCOR 1.47A · GCOR crew & speed

A restriction on a car

The car knocker has put a restriction on one of the Aristech tank cars. What must the conductor do with it?

  • Advise the engineer of the restriction
  • Leave the car where it stands without telling anyone
  • Nothing: the car knocker's tag is enough
  • Tell the PC&Y crew only, when the car is handed over

GCOR 1.47A: the conductor must advise the engineer and train dispatcher of any restriction placed on equipment being handled.

GCOR 1.47A

40 · GCOR 6.13 · Yard limits

No block signals

The East Runner Main is main track inside yard limits, with no block signals. At what speed do you run?

  • 10 MPH, as on a yard track
  • Any speed: yard limits need no protection
  • Restricted speed: able to stop within half the range of vision, not over 20 MPH
  • Track speed, since no train is lined up against you

GCOR 6.13: within yard limits, all movements at restricted speed unless under a block signal more favorable than Approach. GCOR 6.27: restricted speed allows stopping within half the range of vision, looking out for broken rail, not over 20 MPH.

GCOR 6.13

41 · GCOR 5.8.3 · Signals & whistles

The whistle fails

At 10 p.m. #3's whistle fails, and there is no other unit to lead. You still have the main crossing ahead. What now?

  • Continue normally and use the radio at crossings
  • Continue with the bell ringing continuously, and stop before each public crossing so a crew member can warn traffic
  • Run through the crossing quickly to keep clear of traffic
  • Tie up: an engine may not move without a whistle

GCOR 5.8.3: if no other unit can lead, continue with the bell ringing continuously and stop before each public crossing so a crew member can warn traffic, unless the gates are fully down or no traffic is approaching or stopped.

GCOR 5.8.3

42 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

Someone on the track

Pulling the empty ladles west in the dark, you see a man walking on the track ahead, not at a crossing. What does the engineer sound?

  • A succession of short sounds
  • Long, short (— o)
  • Nothing; just ring the bell
  • Two long sounds

GCOR 5.8.2: (1) a succession of short sounds, persons or livestock on the track other than at crossings, or warning employees of an emergency.

GCOR 5.8.2

#305, midnight job a winter night, early 1980s · 7 questions

43 · GCOR 5.8.2 · Signals & whistles

Air in the cold

#3 has pumped up the coke string and the brakeman has finished the air test. The engineer is ready to go. Which whistle signal means release brakes, proceed?

  • One long sound (—)
  • Three short sounds (o o o)
  • Two long sounds (— —)
  • Two short sounds (o o)

GCOR 5.8.2: (3) — —, release brakes, proceed. (2) — is when stopped, air brakes applied, pressure equalized; (5) o o o is back up; (4) o o an acknowledgment.

GCOR 5.8.2

44 · GCOR 5.8.1 · Signals & whistles

A quick move

You make a string of short stop-and-start moves on the coke plant lead. Must the bell be rung before each one?

  • No: momentary stop-and-start switching is excepted
  • Only between midnight and 6:00
  • Only when the whistle has failed
  • Yes, before every movement

GCOR 5.8.1: ring the bell before moving, except momentary stop-and-start switching, as a warning when necessary, approaching men or equipment, and approaching public crossings.

GCOR 5.8.1

45 · GCOR 6.28 · GCOR crew & speed

In the dark

Your headlight lights only a short way into the steam off the quench tower. You take the coke up the furnace lead. What speed?

  • A speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision
  • Not over 10 MPH, whatever the view ahead
  • Restricted speed, not over 20 MPH, looking out for broken rail
  • Yard speed, unless the track is known to be clear

GCOR 6.28: except on a main track or where a block system is in effect, move at a speed that allows stopping within half the range of vision short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment fouling the track, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly.

GCOR 6.28

46 · GCOR 1.47C · GCOR crew & speed

Not slowing

Heading for the West Yard, the brakeman has called a switch lined against you ahead. The engineer, tired at 4:00 a.m., is not slowing. You are in the cab. What must you do?

  • Nothing: running the engine is the engineer's job
  • Remind him at once and, if he still does not act, stop the movement, with the emergency brake valve if necessary
  • Report it to the trainmaster at the end of the shift
  • Wait to see whether he notices in time

GCOR 1.47C: crew members in the engine compartment communicate restrictions and known conditions in time for the engineer to act, and remind him if proper action is not being taken. When the engineer fails to comply, they must immediately take action to ensure safety, using the emergency brake valve to stop the train if necessary.

GCOR 1.47C

47 · GCOR 6.28 · GCOR crew & speed

C9 is frozen

C9 will not come over. You and the brakeman both bar on it and the points stop short of the stock rail. May #3 move over it?

  • No: the move must stop short of a switch lined improperly
  • Yes, at restricted speed
  • Yes, if the brakeman stands on the lever
  • Yes, slowly, and let the wheels push the points over

GCOR 6.28: off main track, move at a speed that allows stopping short of a train, engine, car, men or equipment fouling the track, stop signal, or derail or switch lined improperly.

  • Nothing: plant track has no whistle rules

  • Only at public crossings

67 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-87 · Superiority & movement

Too close to [varies]

You got into the siding at [varies] only [varies] minutes ahead of [varies]'s time there. By how much must an extra clear the time of an opposing regular train?

  • Any margin, as long as it is in the clear
  • Not less than 2 minutes
  • Not less than 5 minutes
  • Only to the leaving time

Rule S-87: extras must clear the time of opposing regular trains by not less than 5 minutes unless otherwise provided. The TT&TO primer quotes 10 minutes.

1949 Standard Code · Rule S-87

[varies] was close behind

[varies] was due to leave the station behind you before you were in the clear at [varies]. When must an inferior train running ahead of a superior train be clear?

  • 5 minutes before the superior train is due at the station ahead
  • At the superior train's arriving time at the station ahead
  • When the superior train comes in sight
  • When the superior train is due to leave the next station in the rear where time is shown

Rule 86: unless otherwise provided, the inferior train must be clear at the time the superior train is due to leave the next station in the rear where time is shown.

  • Slow down and take orders on the fly
  • Stop: an operator is on duty, and you must not leave without a Clearance Form A
  • Whistle — — and keep going

Rule 221: the train order signal shows stop while an operator is on duty, and trains must not leave without a Clearance Form A. The semaphore guide adds that a horizontal blade is always stop.

Check the clearance

  • Only the engineman
  • The conductor, the engineman and the fireman
  • The operator alone

Before leaving Carnegie

Carnegie is your initial station and a register station. What must you find out before Extra 4619 South leaves?

  • The dispatcher's OK on a track warrant
  • Whether all extras on the division have reported clear
  • Whether all superior trains that are due have arrived or left

Rule S-83: a train must not leave its initial station on any division or subdivision, or a junction, or pass from two or more tracks to single track, until it has been ascertained whether all superior trains due have arrived or left. Register stations are designated by time-table, and the train register there records the arrival and departure of trains.

No 92 is a second-class freight. Your train is an extra. Which is superior?

  • No 92: extra trains are inferior to regular trains
  • Your extra, being southward
  • Your extra, since it has no schedule to keep

Rule 73: extra trains are inferior to regular trains. Rule 72: first class is superior to second, second to third.

Who is in charge here?

Your train stands on the main track inside the Carnegie yard limits, and a yardmaster is on duty. Who is in charge of the moves?

  • The conductor of the first train there
  • The dispatcher
  • The engineer of the longest train
  • The yardmaster

75 · Semaphores guide · Semaphores

At Bridgeville, where the Bridgeville & McDonald branch leaves and the P&WV is close by, the home signal of the interlocking shows its blade horizontal.

  • Approach, prepared to stop at the next signal
  • Clear
  • It depends on whether it is upper or lower quadrant
  • Stop

A horizontal semaphore blade is always stop, upper or lower quadrant.

76 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-71 · Superiority & movement

Onto single track

At Houston the line goes from two tracks to one. On single track, how is one train superior to another?

  • By class only
  • By direction, then class, then right
  • By engine number
  • By right, class or direction; right, given by train order, beats class or direction

Rule S-71: right is conferred by train order, class and direction by time-table. Right is superior to class or direction, and direction counts only between trains of the same class.

1949 Standard Code · Rule S-71

77 · 1949 Standard Code · Form S-A · Train orders

The meet order

Your order reads “Extra 4619 South meet Extra 2231 North at Arden.” What does it require?

  • Both trains clear each other's time by 5 minutes at Arden
  • Extra 2231 North waits at Houston for you
  • Neither train may proceed past Arden until both have arrived
  • The train that arrives first goes on at once

Form S-A fixes a meeting point for opposing trains. Neither train may proceed past it until both have arrived. Normally the superior train holds the main and the inferior takes the siding.

1949 Standard Code · Form S-A

78 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 104 · Superiority & movement

The Westland switch

Your head brakeman lined the switch for the Westland branch and the engine took the empties in. Who is responsible for that switch now?

  • Nobody; leave it open for the next train
  • The engineman
  • The section foreman
  • You, the conductor: it must be lined back for the main track

Rule 104: conductors are responsible for the position of switches used by them and their crews, except where switch tenders are stationed. A switch must not be left open for another train unless a member of that train's crew is in charge of it.

1949 Standard Code · Rule 104

79 · Semaphores guide · Semaphores

The signal at Hills

The Montour Railroad joins the line at Hills. The semaphore at the interlocking is an upper-quadrant signal. Through what positions does its blade move?

  • 0° and 90° only
  • 0°, 30° and 60°, dropping
  • 0°, 45° and 90°, rising from horizontal
  • 0°, 60° and 90°

Upper-quadrant blades rise to clear through 0°, 45° and 90°, and came about around 1900. Lower-quadrant blades drop through 0°, 30° and 60°.

Semaphores guide

80 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 99 · Superiority & movement

Standing on the main at Arden

Extra 2231 North has gone by. You pull out of the siding and stop on the main track at Arden while the head brakeman lines the Manifold switch, and a superior train may come up behind you. What protects the rear?

  • The engineman sounds — o o o and the train waits for a reply
  • The flagman drops lighted fusees at intervals until the train moves
  • The flagman goes back at once with flagman's signals, placing two torpedoes and, when necessary, lighted fusees
  • The marker lamps are enough while the switch is being lined

Rule 99: a train stopped where it may be overtaken is protected by the flagman going back immediately with flagman's signals a sufficient distance to insure full protection, placing two torpedoes and, when necessary, lighted fusees. The engineman signals the flagman to go back, and recalls him when ready to proceed.

1949 Standard Code · Rule 99

81 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule S-88 · Superiority & movement

Meeting Extra 2231 North

Extra 2231 North is at Arden, and your order says the two extras meet there. Northward trains are superior by direction. Which extra takes the siding?

  • Extra 2231 North, because it is the opposing train
  • Extra 4619 South, the train in the inferior time-table direction
  • The one with the higher engine number
  • Whichever arrives first

Rule S-88: when two extras meet, the train in the inferior time-table direction takes the siding, unless otherwise provided. On Form S-A, neither train goes past Arden until both have arrived.

1949 Standard Code · Rule S-88

82 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule D-71 · Superiority & movement

The double track

From Carnegie to Houston the line is double track. On two or more tracks, how is a train superior?

  • By class or direction
  • By direction only
  • By right or class only; direction no longer counts
  • By right, class or direction, as on single track

Rule D-71: on two or more tracks a train is superior by right or class only. Right is conferred by train order, class by time-table, and right is superior to class. The S- rules are the single-track versions.

1949 Standard Code · Rule D-71

83 · Semaphores guide · Semaphores

An old lower-quadrant blade

The fireman notes the next signal is a lower-quadrant semaphore. Why is a lower-quadrant blade not fail-safe?

  • If the mechanism fails, gravity drops the blade toward a proceed position
  • It can show only two positions
  • Its lamp burns out easily
  • Snow freezes it at stop

On a lower-quadrant signal the blade drops to clear (0°, 30°, 60°), so a broken linkage can turn stop into approach or clear. Upper-quadrant blades rise (0°, 45°, 90°).

Semaphores guide

84 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 99 · Superiority & movement

Slow on the grade

Extra 4619 is crawling up a grade, and a superior train may come up behind you while you are still moving. How does the flagman protect the rear?

  • He drops lighted fusees at proper intervals
  • He goes back and places two torpedoes while the train keeps moving
  • None is needed while the train is moving
  • The engineman sounds — o o o every mile

Rule 99: a moving train that may be overtaken is protected by the flagman dropping lighted fusees at proper intervals. Torpedoes are for a stopped train.

1949 Standard Code · Rule 99

Behind the blade

The colored glass lenses on a semaphore are the roundels. What holds them?

  • The blade
  • The housing
  • The lamp
  • The spectacle

Semaphore parts: blade, roundels (the lenses), spectacle (holds the roundels), lamp, actuating mechanism, housing.

Semaphores guide

86 · Semaphores guide · Semaphores

Fixed at 45 degrees

Before a river bridge stands a semaphore whose blade never moves from 45°. What is it?

  • A single-position signal: a permanent approach warning of something ahead
  • A stop signal
  • A train order board

Single-position semaphores were fixed at 45° as a permanent warning of something ahead such as a bridge, commonly for a restricting indication.

Semaphores guide

87 · Semaphores guide · Semaphores

Old signals

The fireman says these semaphores are as old as the railroad. When was the semaphore patented?

  • Around 1900
  • In the 1840s
  • In the 1870s
  • In the 1930s

The semaphore was patented in the 1840s and first lit by kerosene, later by electric bulbs. The upper quadrant came around 1900.

Semaphores guide

The switch at the north end of this siding is blocked by a car, so you must back into the siding from the south end. What does Rule S-89 require?

  • Nothing, if the superior train is not in sight
  • Protect the train as prescribed by Rule 99

The operator says yesterday's No 304, a regular train, is more than 12 hours behind its schedule at this station. What is its standing now?

  • It has lost both right and schedule and may move only by train order
  • It keeps its schedule but loses right
  • It runs on its schedule at restricted speed

Word comes of a southward freight disabled ahead and unable to move. If needed, your train may…

  • Push it to the next siding

  • The southward train, which is running late

Rule S-72: trains in the direction specified by the time-table are superior to trains of the same class in the opposite direction. On the Chartiers Branch time-table that is northward.

Rule 72: trains of the first class are superior to those of the second, second to third, and so on.

  • Second 305 waits 10 minutes

  • Yes, if the dispatcher says so by phone

Rule 92: a train must not leave a station in advance of its schedule leaving time.

95 · 1949 Standard Code · Rule 20 · Superiority & movement

Two green flags

  • It has right over all trains
  • It is running late
  • The track ahead is clear for two blocks

  • It gives your train right over both trains
  • It is not a proper form; each meet needs its own order
  • It requires your train to take the siding at Houston and at Tylerdale

  • The extra must wait at Tylerdale 10 minutes
  • Your train has right over the extra to Tylerdale
  • Your train must take the siding at Tylerdale

Form S-A fixes a meeting point for opposing trains. Neither train may proceed past it until both have arrived. Normally the superior train holds the main and the inferior takes the siding.

  • The meet at Arden is superseded; the meet is at Houston
  • There are now two meets, at Arden and at Houston
  • You wait at Arden, then at Houston

Form S-P: “instead of” supersedes an order. A superseded order is not reissued under its original number. Any part of an order specifying a particular movement may be superseded or annulled (Rule 220).

  • A signal of fixed location indicating a condition affecting the movement of a train or engine

  • Proceed at restricted speed
  • Proceed preparing to stop at next signal. Train exceeding medium speed must at once reduce to that speed

Rule 285, Approach: Proceed preparing to stop at next signal. Train exceeding medium speed must at once reduce to that speed.

  • Maximum authorized speed
